claim: Different human diseases, such as several imprinting-associated syndromes (Angelman syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome), arise due to the inheritance of parental information that is not encoded in the DNA sequence.
source: Different human diseases, such as several imprinting-associated syndromes (Angelman syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome), arise due to the inheritance of parental information that is not encoded in the DNA sequence (Tucci et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tucci et al., 2019.

claim: Many widespread disorders were suggested to be influenced by non-genetic inheritance and to be affected by the ancestors' life history.
source: Furthermore, and although the underlying mechanisms are still unclear, many widespread disorders were suggested to be influenced by non-genetic inheritance and to be affected by the ancestors' life history (Bohacek and Mansuy, 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Gapp et al., 2014; Kazachenka et al., 2018; Nilsson et al., 2018; Öst et al., 2014; Skvortsova et al., 2018; Teperino et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Small RNA inheritance factors, which are specifically required for the regulation of heritable responses, have been identified in C. elegans.
source: Small RNA inheritance factors, which are specifically required for the regulation of heritable responses, have been identified (Ashe et al., 2012; Buckley et al., 2012; de Albuquerque et al., 2015; Houri-Ze'evi et al., 2016; Lev et al., 2019b; Lev et al., 2017; Shirayama et al., 2012; Wan et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Specific worm Argonaute proteins (HRDE-1, CSR-1, WAGO-4, WAGO-1) physically carry small RNAs in the germline and across generations.
source: and specific worm Argonaute proteins (HRDE-1, CSR-1, WAGO-4, WAGO-1) were found to physically carry small RNAs in the germline and across generations (Ashe et al., 2012; Claycomb et al., 2009; Shirayama et al., 2012; Wedeles et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The multigenerational small RNA inheritance response requires RNA-dependent RNA Polymerases (RdRPs) which use the target mRNA as a template for amplifying 'secondary' or 'amplified' small RNAs.
source: The multigenerational small RNA inheritance response requires RNA-dependent RNA Polymerases (RdRPs) which use the target mRNA as a template for amplifying 'secondary' or 'amplified' small RNAs (Rechavi et al., 2011; Sapetschnig et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The amplification reaction outcompetes the dilution of the heritable small RNA molecules in every generation and enables the transgenerational transmission of small RNAs.
source: The amplification reaction outcompetes the dilution of the heritable small RNA molecules in every generation and enables the transgenerational transmission of small RNAs (Rechavi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Amplification of heritable small RNAs can be induced by multiple 'primary' small RNA species, of both exogenous and endogenous sources – such as small interfering RNAs and PIWI-interacting RNAs.
source: Amplification of heritable small RNAs can be induced by multiple 'primary' small RNA species, of both exogenous and endogenous sources – such as small interfering RNAs and PIWI-interacting RNAs (Das et al., 2008; Sijen et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Amplification of transgenerationally inherited small RNAs occurs in germ granules.
source: Amplification of transgenerationally inherited small RNAs occurs in germ granules (Dodson and Kennedy, 2019; Lev et al., 2019b; Ouyang et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Germ granules are cytoplasmic condensates made of RNA and proteins found in germ cells of many organisms.
source: cytoplasmic condensates made of RNA and proteins found in germ cells of many organisms (Brangwynne et al., 2009; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017; Voronina et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In the nucleus, amplified small RNAs lead to transcriptional silencing of their targets in cooperation with chromatin regulators.
source: In the nucleus, amplified small RNAs lead to transcriptional silencing of their targets in cooperation with chromatin regulators (Burton et al., 2011; Kalinava et al., 2017; Lev et al., 2019a; Lev et al., 2017; She et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Nuclear small RNAs promote modification of chromatin, and some changes in histone marks are transgenerationally inherited, also in response to environmental changes.
source: Nuclear small RNAs promote modification of chromatin, and some changes in histone marks are transgenerationally inherited, also in response to environmental changes (Klosin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The worm's small RNA pools can change transgenerationally in response to multiple environmental challenges such as viral and bacterial infection, starvation, and stressful temperatures.
source: The worm's small RNA pools can change transgenerationally in response to multiple environmental challenges such as viral and bacterial infection (Kaletsky et al., 2020; Moore et al., 2019; Rechavi et al., 2011), starvation (Ewe et al., 2020; Rechavi et al., 2014), and stressful temperatures (Ni et al., 2016; Schott et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: C. elegans actively regulates small RNA inheritance and controls the duration and potency of the transgenerational effects across generations.
source: Further, C. elegans actively regulates small RNA inheritance and controls the duration and potency of the transgenerational effects across generations (Houri-Ze'evi et al., 2016; Houri-Zeevi and Rechavi, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Heritable RNA interference (RNAi) responses can be induced by targeting germline-expressed genes using double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) triggers.
source: Heritable RNA interference (RNAi) responses, which are mediated by small RNAs, can be induced by targeting germline-expressed genes using double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) triggers.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about RNAi in C. elegans.

claim: At the population level, heritable RNAi responses typically last three to five generations.
source: Typically, at the population level, such heritable responses last three to five generations (Alcazar et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The duration of the heritable response varies among different individuals and in mutants of epigenetic factors.
source: but the duration of the heritable response varies among different individuals (Houri-Zeevi et al., 2020) and in mutants of epigenetic factors (Houri-Ze'evi et al., 2016; Perales et al., 2018; Spracklin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: MET-2 is a putative histone 3 lysine 9 (H3K9) methyltransferase and the homologue of mammalian SETDB1.
source: For example, MET-2, a putative histone 3 lysine 9 (H3K9) methyltransferase and the homologue of mammalian SETDB1
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about MET-2.

claim: MET-2 is required for termination of heritable RNAi responses and reestablishment of the zygote's epigenetic ground state.
source: is required for termination of heritable RNAi responses and reestablishment of the zygote's epigenetic ground state.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about MET-2's function.

claim: RNAi inheritance is stable in met-2 mutants and is not diminished across generations.
source: Accordingly, RNAi inheritance is stable in met-2 mutants and is not diminished across generations (Kerr et al., 2014; Lev et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The inheritance of ancestral RNAi responses can be extended by triggering dsRNA-induced silencing of other genes in the progeny.
source: Even in wild-type animals, the inheritance of ancestral RNAi responses can be extended by triggering dsRNA-induced silencing of other genes in the progeny (Houri-Ze'evi et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The inheritance of ancestral RNAi responses can be extended by selecting lineages of worms which have stronger heritable effects.
source: and by selecting lineages of worms which have stronger heritable effects (Houri-Zeevi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Mutants that are unable to regulate the multigenerational accumulation of heritable small RNAs become sterile.
source: Indeed, in worms, mutants that are unable to regulate the multigenerational accumulation of heritable small RNAs become sterile (Lev et al., 2019b; Lev et al., 2017; Ni et al., 2016; Simon et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Stress leads to a strong reduction of heritable gfp silencing within the same generation (F1) and in the next generations that were not directly exposed to stress (F2-F5).
source: We found that stress during the L1 stage led to a strong reduction of heritable gfp silencing within the same generation (F1) and in the next generations that were not directly exposed to stress (F2-F5, in the F6 generation the heritable response was generally lost in all groups – in accordance with the bottleneck of inheritance. See Figure 1, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Stress during adulthood leads to resetting of heritable silencing in the next generation.
source: We found that, as was observed when stress was applied during the L1 stage, stress during adulthood leads to resetting of heritable silencing in the next generation (q < 0.0001, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: When stress was applied two generations after the parental exposure to dsRNA, no statistically significant stress-induced resetting was detected.
source: In contrast, when stress was applied two generations after the parental exposure to dsRNA (P0: initiation of inheritance, F1: no stress, F2: stress), we did not detect statistically significant stress-induced resetting (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The fate of the heritable response (its persistence across generations) is determined at the first generations.
source: We previously showed that the fate of the heritable response (its persistence across generations) is determined at the first generations (Houri-Zeevi et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Re-challenging the F1 generation – but not the F2 generation – with RNAi extends the duration of ancestral RNAi responses.
source: and that re-challenging the F1 generation – but not the F2 generation – with RNAi extends the duration of ancestral RNAi responses (Houri-Zeevi and Rechavi, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: There exists a critical period at the F1 generation, during which the heritable response is still plastic and can be modified by external perturbations.
source: Together, these results indicate the existence of a critical period at the F1 generation, during which the heritable response is still plastic and can be modified by external perturbations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that stress at F1 but not F2 affects inheritance.

claim: All three stressors (Heat, Osmotic, and Starvation stress) reset both endo-siRNAs- and piRNAs-mediated heritable silencing in worms that were directly exposed to stress.
source: We found that all three stressors (Heat, Osmotic, and Starvation stress) reset both endo-siRNAs- and piRNAs-mediated heritable silencing in worms that were directly exposed to stress (Dunn's test, q-value <0.0005 and q-value <0.0007, respectively. See Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Unstressed worms in the next generations re-established endo-siRNAs- and piRNAs-mediated silencing.
source: However, in contrast to exo-siRNAs-mediated silencing that was reset in a transgenerational manner (Figure 1C), we found that unstressed worms in the next generations re-established endo-siRNAs- and piRNAs-mediated silencing.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing exo-siRNAs and endo-siRNAs/piRNAs responses.

claim: Primary endo-siRNAs and piRNAs are encoded in the genome and do not depend on exogenous sources for their existence.
source: Unlike exogenous primary small RNAs which cannot be re-synthesized in the progeny, primary endo-siRNAs and piRNAs are encoded in the genome and do not depend on exogenous sources for their existence (Ambros et al., 2003; Cecere et al., 2012; Duchaine et al., 2006; Gu et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2006; Lemmens and Tijsterman, 2011; Ruby et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The re-establishment of endo-siRNAs and piRNAs-mediated silencing in the next generations after stress indicates that these small RNAs can be transcribed de novo at each generation.
source: The re-establishment of endo-siRNAs and piRNAs-mediated silencing in the next generations after stress indicates that these small RNAs can be transcribed de novo at each generation, and thus can compensate for stress-induced erasure of parental small RNA molecules
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observation of re-establishment of silencing.

claim: There is a fundamental difference in the 'memory programs' of exogenous and endogenous transgenerational small RNA responses.
source: suggesting a fundamental difference in the 'memory programs' of exogenous and endogenous transgenerational small RNA responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the different behaviors of exogenous and endogenous small RNA responses to stress.

claim: Resetting only occurs in response to stress; progeny of stressed worms that were transferred to non-stressful conditions did not exhibit resetting of the heritable response.
source: We found that resetting only occurs in response to stress (q-value <0.0001, Figure 3A); Progeny of stressed worms that were transferred to non-stressful conditions did not exhibit resetting of the heritable response.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Two consecutive generations of mild stress led to a weaker inheritance compared to worms that were not exposed to stress at all.
source: Moreover, two consecutive generations of mild stress led to a weaker inheritance compared to worms that were not exposed to stress at all (q-value <0.0001, Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: RNAi responses initiated in stressed parents were strengthened when the progeny were transferred to non-stressful conditions.
source: and RNAi responses initiated in stressed parents were strengthened when the progeny were transferred to non-stressful conditions (q-value <0.0053, Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Stress, and not any change in growth conditions, leads to the resetting of heritable small RNA responses, even regardless of the ancestral growth conditions.
source: Overall, we conclude that stress, and not any change in growth conditions, leads to the resetting of heritable small RNA responses, even regardless of the ancestral growth conditions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that only stress, not environmental change, causes resetting.

claim: Exposure to stress (starvation), even prior to the initiation of inheritance (for either one or three consecutive generations), leads to a similar resetting response as observed for stress that is applied in the next generation.
source: Instead, we found that exposure to stress (starvation), even prior to the initiation of inheritance (for either one or three consecutive generations), leads to a similar resetting response as observed for stress that is applied in the next generation (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Stress inheritance can compete with other transgenerational responses, or affect the function of small RNA machinery in a transgenerational manner.
source: These results indicate that stress inheritance can in fact compete with other transgenerational responses, or, alternatively, affect the function of small RNA machinery in a transgenerational manner (see Figure 3B and Discussion).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that pre-exposure to stress affects later heritable responses.

claim: All three types of stress conditions led to a reduction in the levels of heritable endogenous small RNA in worms that were directly exposed to stress.
source: Consistently with the observed phenotypic resetting of heritable responses following stress, in worms that were directly exposed to stress, all three types of stress conditions led to a reduction in the levels of heritable endogenous small RNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data.

claim: Different stressors shaped the small RNA pools of the next generation in different ways.
source: However, across multiple repeats (see Materials and methods), different stressors shaped the small RNA pools of the next generation in different ways (Figure 4B)
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Starvation stress led to a reduction in endogenous small RNA levels both in the worms that were directly exposed to stress and in their progeny.
source: starvation stress led to a reduction in endogenous small RNA levels both in the worms that were directly exposed to stress and in their progeny.
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data.

claim: Heat stress caused a reduction in endogenous small RNA levels in the stressed generation, but most types of endogenous small RNA showed elevated levels in the next generation after heat stress.
source: In contrast, heat stress caused a reduction in endogenous small RNA levels in the stressed generation, but most types of endogenous small RNA showed elevated levels in the next generation after heat stress (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No consistent heritable change in the global levels of endogenous small RNAs was detected following hyperosmotic stress.
source: We did not detect a consistent heritable change in the global levels of endogenous small RNAs following hyperosmotic stress (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 281 genes were identified as being targeted by stress-affected endogenous small RNAs.
source: To better explore how stress-induced resetting affects each pathway, we examined stress-induced changes in small RNA regulation over specific genes and identified a list of 281 genes that were targeted by stress-affected endogenous small RNAs (regardless of the stress type. FDR < 0.1, Figure 4C and D, Supplementary file 1 and Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The targets of stress-affected small RNAs show enrichment for stress-related functions.
source: Interestingly, the targets of these stress-affected small RNAs show enrichment for stress-related functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of the identified gene targets.

claim: Stress-affected small RNA target genes were shown to be regulated by the TGF-beta pathway and the insulin pathway, and to be affected in response to rapamycin exposure and changes in temperature.
source: As a group, these genes were shown to be regulated by the TGF-beta pathway and the insulin pathway, and to be affected in response to rapamycin exposure and changes in temperature (Calvert et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2015; Shaw et al., 2007; Viñuela et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In most of the gene targets of stress-affected small RNAs (202/281, 72%) the targeting small RNAs were down-regulated, or 'reset', following stress.
source: In agreement with the observed overall reduction in endogenous small RNA levels and the phenotypic resetting of the silencing responses, in most of the gene targets of stress-affected small RNAs (202/281, 72%) the targeting small RNAs were down-regulated, or 'reset', following stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: Endogenous small RNAs that were reset following stress exhibited a strong enrichment for hrde-1-dependent small RNAs and Mutator-dependent small RNAs.
source: These endogenous small RNAs exhibited a strong enrichment for hrde-1-dependent small RNAs and Mutator-dependent small RNAs (Phillips et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2011) (see Figure 4C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 4C and E.

claim: The HRDE-1 (Heritable RNAi Deficient-1) Argonaute is an important regulator of transgenerational gene silencing by small RNAs and is explicitly required for transmission of silencing responses across generations.
source: The HRDE-1 (Heritable RNAi Deficient-1) Argonaute is an important regulator of transgenerational gene silencing by small RNAs and, while largely dispensable for silencing within the same generation, is explicitly required for transmission of silencing responses across generations (Ashe et al., 2012; Buckley et al., 2012; Shirayama et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The Mutator proteins are involved in multiple endogenous small RNA biogenesis pathways, affecting both somatic and germline small RNAs, and are required for efficient small RNA amplification and cleavage of target RNAs.
source: The Mutator proteins (mut-16, mut-14;smut-1 Phillips et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2011) were shown to be involved in multiple endogenous small RNA biogenesis pathways, affecting both somatic and germline small RNAs, and are required for efficient small RNA amplification and cleavage of target RNAs (rde-8 and nyn-1;nyn-2 Tsai et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Generating mut-14;smut-1;mut-16 triple mutants enables erasure of heritable small RNA-based memory of self and non-self-genes.
source: Generating (via crossing) mut-14;smut-1;mut-16 triple mutants was previously shown to enable erasure of heritable small RNA-based memory of self and non-self-genes (de Albuquerque et al., 2015; Phillips et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Targets of stress-reduced small RNAs are enriched for dsRNA-producing loci and piRNAs gene targets.
source: Additionally, we found here that targets of stress-reduced small RNAs are enriched for dsRNA-producing loci (Saldi et al., 2014) and piRNAs gene targets (Bagijn et al., 2012) (see the full list of enrichments in Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by enrichment analysis of small RNA sequencing data.

claim: The targets of small RNAs that showed elevated levels following stress (79/281, 28%) were almost exclusively CSR-1-dependent endo-siRNAs.
source: In contrast to the enrichment of HRDE-1 and Mutator-dependent small RNAs among small RNAs which are reset following stress, the targets of small RNAs that showed elevated levels of small RNAs following stress (79/281, 28%) were almost exclusively CSR-1-dependent endo-siRNAs (hypergeometric test, p-value=2.9 e−48, 96% were found to be physically bound to CSR-1, Claycomb et al., 2009; Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Endo-siRNAs which are bound by the CSR-1 Argonaute promote gene expression rather than gene silencing in the worms.
source: Unlike other endo-siRNAs pathways, endo-siRNAs which are bound by the CSR-1 Argonaute were demonstrated to promote gene expression rather than gene silencing in the worms (Wedeles et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Only 10 genes were targeted by small RNAs that showed widespread changes in the progeny of stressed worms, when accounting for all stress types together.
source: Finally, we did not detect widespread changes in stress-affected small RNAs in the progeny of stressed worms, when accounting for all stress types together (only 10 genes were targeted by such small RNAs, Supplementary file 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: Multiple epigenetic, small RNA, and p-granules factors consistently show significantly reduced gene expression levels following stress, regardless of the stress types.
source: We found that multiple epigenetic, small RNA, and p-granules factors consistently show significantly reduced gene expression levels following stress, regardless of the stress types (73 epigenetic-related genes significantly downregulated in all stress conditions with FDR < 0.1, Supplementary file 4, hypergeometric test; fold-enrichment = 2.4, adjusted p-value<0.00001).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of published mRNA-sequencing data.

claim: The Argonaute genes hrde-1, rde-1, ergo-1, nrde-3, wago-1, and alg-2 are all significantly downregulated across all stress types.
source: Specifically, we found that the Argonaute genes hrde-1, rde-1, ergo-1, nrde-3, wago-1, and alg-2 are all significantly downregulated across all stress types.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of published mRNA-sequencing data.

claim: The Argonautes hrde-1, rde-1, ergo-1, nrde-3, wago-1, and alg-2 regulate and are necessary for RNAi responses both within and across generations.
source: These Argonautes were previously shown to regulate and be necessary for RNAi responses both within and across generations (Buckley et al., 2012; Billi et al., 2014; Grishok et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The Mutator genes mut-2 and mut-16, and the factors rde-4, rrf-3, hrde-4, and rde-8 all show significantly reduced gene expression levels in response to stress.
source: Additionally, we found that the Mutator genes mut-2 and mut-16, whose small RNAs were depleted following stress, and the factors rde-4, rrf-3, hrde-4, and rde-8 all show significantly reduced gene expression levels in response to stress (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of published mRNA-sequencing data.

claim: The epigenetic factors rde-4, rrf-3, hrde-4, and rde-8 are required for the synthesis, amplification, and inheritance of small RNAs across generations.
source: These epigenetic factors were previously found to be required for the synthesis, amplification, and inheritance of small RNAs across generations (Duchaine et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2006; Parker, 2006; Spracklin et al., 2017; Tabara et al., 2002; Tsai et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Stress induces a widespread suppression of various components of the small RNA machinery.
source: Overall, we find that stress induces a widespread suppression of various components of the small RNA machinery, in accordance with the observed global resetting of small RNA responses and multiple types of endogenous small RNAs (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mRNA-seq data analysis showing downregulation of small RNA machinery components.

claim: Eight mutants defective in stress responses showed a general enhanced or defective RNAi inheritance, irrespectively of whether the mutant worms experienced stress or not.
source: Interestingly, out of the 11 mutants defective in stress responses that we examined, eight mutants showed a general enhanced (pmk-1/p38 MAPK, sek-1/p38 MAP2K, skn-1/Nrf2, daf-2/InsR) or defective (mek-1;sek-1, kgb-1, daf-2/InsR;daf-16/FOXO, hsf-1/HSF1) RNAi inheritance (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2). This was true irrespectively of whether the mutant worms experienced stress or not
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Stress regulation and small RNA inheritance are interconnected even in the absence of stress.
source: and suggests that stress regulation and small RNA inheritance are interconnected even in the absence of stress.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that stress pathway mutants show altered RNAi inheritance even without stress.

claim: MAP Kinase (MAPK) genes (sek-1/mek-1, sek-1, pmk-1, kgb-1), and the skn-1 gene are required for resetting of RNAi inheritance in response to stress.
source: We found that MAP Kinase (MAPK) genes (sek-1/mek-1, sek-1, pmk-1, kgb-1), and the skn-1 gene are required for resetting of RNAi inheritance in response to stress (Figure 5B and C, and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C, and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: skn-1/Nrf2 encodes a transcription factor which is regulated by p38 MAPK-dependent phosphorylation.
source: skn-1/Nrf2 encodes a transcription factor which is regulated by p38 MAPK-dependent phosphorylation (Inoue et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: All the examined mutant worms expressed the GFP transgene in similar levels to wild-type worms in the absence of anti-gfp RNAi response.
source: Importantly, all the examined mutant worms expressed the GFP transgene in similar levels to wild-type worms in the absence of anti-gfp RNAi response (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: HSF-1 activity corresponds to the 'inheritance state' of worms when initiating a heritable RNAi response.
source: We recently showed that HSF-1 activity corresponds to the 'inheritance state' of worms when initiating a heritable RNAi response (Houri-Zeevi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: The finding that hsf-1 mutants are capable of resetting RNAi inheritance in response to stress suggests that HSF-1's role is likely in the initiation, and not the maintenance, of heritable RNAi responses.
source: Our finding that hsf-1 mutants are capable of resetting RNAi inheritance in response to stress suggests that HSF-1's role is likely in the initiation, and not the maintenance, of heritable RNAi responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental observation that hsf-1 mutants can still reset RNAi inheritance.

claim: The MAPK pathway is necessary for the integration of responses to multiple types of stress, such as DNA damage, osmotic stress, heat shock, and pathogen infection.
source: The MAPK pathway is necessary for the integration of responses to multiple types of stress, such as DNA damage (Bianco and Schumacher, 2018; Ermolaeva et al., 2013), osmotic stress (Gerke et al., 2014), heat shock (Mertenskötter et al., 2013), and pathogen infection (Troemel et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The ability to reset heritable responses following stress, and the ability to transmit RNAi, appear to be two distinct functions.
source: Interestingly, we found that the ability to reset heritable responses following stress, and the ability to transmit RNAi, appear to be two distinct functions
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that different mutants show different patterns of RNAi inheritance and resetting.

claim: Some of the mutants that did not reset heritable silencing following stress showed enhanced RNAi inheritance (sek-1, pmk-1, skn-1, acting in the same signaling cascade), while others were defective in RNAi inheritance (mek-1/sek-1 and kgb-1).
source: some of the mutants that did not reset heritable silencing following stress showed enhanced RNAi inheritance (sek-1, pmk-1, skn-1, acting in the same signaling cascade), while others were defective in RNAi inheritance (mek-1/sek-1 and kgb-1) (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Resetting of heritable silencing following stress is a regulated process that is mediated by the MAPK pathway and by the skn-1 transcription factor.
source: Overall, we conclude that resetting of heritable silencing following stress is a regulated process that is mediated by the MAPK pathway and by the skn-1 transcription factor.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that MAPK pathway and skn-1 mutants cannot reset RNAi inheritance.

claim: Neuronal expression of sek-1 is sufficient to re-establish a strong resetting of silencing in response to stress.
source: We found that neuronal expression of sek-1 is sufficient to re-establish a strong resetting of silencing in response to stress (Figure 5D, Cliff's Delta = 0.4597, 0.593, 0.2672 for heat stress, hyperosmotic stress, and starvation stress, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Intestinal rescue of sek-1 did not regenerate a strong resetting response following heat stress and starvation stress, but did regenerate a strong resetting response following osmotic stress.
source: Intestinal rescue of sek-1, on the other hand, did not regenerate a strong resetting response following heat stress and starvation stress (Cliff's Delta = 0.0905, 0.0909), but did regenerate a strong resetting response following osmotic stress (Cliff's Delta = 0.4108).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with effect size measurements.

claim: Osmotic stress is the only stress condition that did not show a consistent effect on the total small RNA pools in unstressed progeny.
source: Notably, osmotic stress is the only stress condition that did not show a consistent effect on the total small RNA pools in unstressed progeny (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Unlike starvation and heat stress, osmotic stress was shown to elicit an intergenerational, and not a transgenerational, epigenetic response.
source: Moreover, unlike starvation and heat stress, osmotic stress was shown to elicit an intergenerational, and not a transgenerational, epigenetic response (Burton et al., 2017; Rechavi et al., 2014; Schott et al., 2015), that is mediated through the intestine.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: While many stress-related factors in the worm affect the basic function of the RNAi inheritance machinery, the p38 MAPK pathway – and the SKN-1/Nrf2 transcription factor which is regulated by it – are specifically required for resetting of small RNAs in response to stress.
source: Overall, we conclude that while many stress-related factors in the worm affect the basic function of the RNAi inheritance machinery (Figure 5A), the p38 MAPK pathway – and the SKN-1/Nrf2 transcription factor which is regulated by it – are specifically required for resetting of small RNAs in response to stress.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing specific requirements for MAPK pathway and SKN-1 in stress-induced resetting.

claim: SKN-1 could function in stress-induced resetting of small RNAs by directly regulating the expression of various epigenetic and small RNA factors.
source: It is therefore plausible that SKN-1 could function in stress-induced resetting of small RNAs by directly regulating the expression of various epigenetic and small RNA factors.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about SKN-1's potential mechanism of action.

claim: Recent findings have implicated SKN-1 in transgenerational inheritance in C. elegans.
source: Moreover, recent findings have implicated SKN-1 in transgenerational inheritance in C. elegans (Burton et al., 2020; Ewe et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Genes that are normally repressed in response to stress but show significantly weaker repression in anti-skn-1 RNAi background are significantly enriched for epigenetic genes and p-granule factors.
source: We found that this group of genes is significantly enriched for epigenetic genes and p-granule factors (599 genes, 35 of which are epigenetic-related genes; q-values = 0.000134, 0.00680, Supplementary files 5 and 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of published mRNA-sequencing data.

claim: The Argonaute gene nrde-3 and the epigenetic factors rrf-3, rde-8, and nyn-2 are downregulated in response to stress in a skn-1-dependent manner.
source: In particular, we found that the Argonaute gene nrde-3 and the epigenetic factors rrf-3, rde-8, and nyn-2 are downregulated in response to stress in a skn-1-dependent manner, in accordance with the epigenetic factors we found to be downregulated in response to all stress conditions (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of published mRNA-sequencing data.

claim: Among the epigenetic genes whose promoter regions contained SKN-1 binding sites were the putative RNA-dependent RNA polymerase rrf-3 and the putative H3K9 histone methyltransferase met-2.
source: Among the epigenetic genes whose promoter regions contained SKN-1 binding sites (63 genes) were the putative RNA-dependent RNA polymerase rrf-3 and the putative H3K9 histone methyltransferase met-2 (p-value=0.0001, 0.0001, Supplementary file 7; Pujato et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of SKN-1 binding motifs in promoter regions.

claim: SKN-1 could affect the expression of multiple epigenetic and small RNA factors, including factors that were previously shown to regulate the duration of heritable RNAi responses.
source: Overall, we conclude that SKN-1 could affect the expression of multiple epigenetic and small RNA factors, including factors that were previously shown to regulate the duration of heritable RNAi responses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the analysis of SKN-1 binding sites and gene expression data.

claim: Stress leads to the resetting of transgenerationally transmitted small RNAs, erasing heritable gene regulatory responses.
source: In this study, we found that stress leads to the resetting of transgenerationally transmitted small RNAs, erasing heritable gene regulatory responses.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Stress-induced resetting depends on the p38 MAPK pathway and the SKN-1 transcription factor.
source: Stress-induced resetting depends on the p38 MAPK pathway and the SKN-1 transcription factor
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data with mutants.

claim: Stress-induced resetting is regulated by MET-2, a putative H3K9 methyltransferase that is required for germline reprogramming.
source: and is regulated by MET-2, a putative H3K9 methyltransferase that is required for germline reprogramming (Kerr et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data with met-2 mutants.

claim: Stress induces a reduction in small RNA levels across the genome.
source: We found that stress induces a reduction in small RNA levels across the genome.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the small RNA sequencing data.

claim: The reduction in small RNA levels following stress stems from changes in multiple distinct small RNA species, including small RNAs that regulate stress-related genes.
source: This reduction stems from changes in multiple distinct small RNA species, including small RNAs that regulate stress-related genes.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the small RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: A mechanism for resetting of heritable small RNAs could be adaptive in rapidly changing environments.
source: We speculate that a mechanism for resetting of heritable small RNAs could be adaptive in rapidly changing environments (see model in Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential adaptive significance of the findings.

claim: Active removal of epigenetic regulation in response to stress could serve as a mechanism for increasing genetic and phenotypic variability.
source: Active removal of epigenetic regulation in response to stress could serve as a mechanism for increasing genetic and phenotypic variability.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential function of stress-induced resetting.

claim: Small RNAs in C. elegans distinguish between self and non-self-genes.
source: Small RNAs in C. elegans distinguish between self and non-self-genes (Shirayama et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Small RNAs orchestrate gene expression in the germline and during development.
source: and orchestrate gene expression in the germline and during development (Feng and Guang, 2013; Gu et al., 2009; Han et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Relieving the regulation of heritable small RNAs could be a way to increase phenotypic plasticity or to reveal hidden genetic variability.
source: Relieving the regulation of heritable small RNAs could be a way to increase phenotypic plasticity or to reveal hidden genetic variability.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential consequences of stress-induced resetting.

claim: A conserved microRNA in flies was shown to buffer developmental programs against variation.
source: For example, a conserved microRNA in flies was shown to buffer developmental programs against variation (Li et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Changes in neuronal small RNA levels generate transgenerational effects.
source: We have recently found that changes in neuronal small RNA levels generate transgenerational effects (Posner et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Olfactory memory can become heritable.
source: Similarly, it has been shown that olfactory memory can become heritable (Moore et al., 2019; Pereira et al., 2019; Remy, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The systemic response to stress that KGB-1, SKN-1, and SEK-1 mediate was shown to be coordinated by the nervous system.
source: The systemic response to stress that KGB-1, SKN-1, and SEK-1 mediate (factors which are shown here to be required for resetting) was shown in the past to be coordinated by the nervous system (Bishop and Guarente, 2007; Liu et al., 2018; Shivers et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: MET-2 is essential for termination of RNAi inheritance and establishment of an epigenetic 'ground state'.
source: In previous studies, it was shown that MET-2, a putative histone methyltransferase required for mono- and di-methylation of H3K9 and the homologue of mammalian SETDB1, is essential for termination of RNAi inheritance and establishment of an epigenetic 'ground state' (Garrigues et al., 2015; Greer et al., 2014; Kerr et al., 2014; Lev et al., 2017; Mutlu et al., 2018; Towbin et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In met-2 mutants aberrant endo-siRNAs accumulate over generations, eventually leading to sterility (Mortal Germline, Mrt phenotype).
source: and that in met-2 mutants aberrant endo-siRNAs accumulate over generations, eventually leading to sterility (Mortal Germline, Mrt phenotype) (Andersen and Horvitz, 2007; Lev et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Targets of stress-affected small RNAs were enriched for genes which were previously found to be misregulated in met-2 mutants.
source: Examination of published datasets revealed that targets of stress-affected small RNAs were enriched for genes which were previously found to be misregulated in met-2 mutants (FDR = 2.1e-05) (Zeller et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of published datasets.

claim: Targets of stress-affected small RNAs have significantly higher than expected levels of H3K9me2.
source: and that these genes have significantly higher than expected levels of H3K9me2 (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of published ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: met-2's expression levels are significantly downregulated in worms under heat stress, osmotic stress, and starvation stress.
source: Furthermore, we observe that met-2's expression levels are significantly downregulated in worms under heat stress, osmotic stress, and starvation stress (q-values = 0.002211, 0.048440, 0.048440).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of published mRNA-sequencing data.

claim: MET-2 is essential for stress-induced resetting of heritable RNAi.
source: Interestingly, we also observed that MET-2 is essential for stress-induced resetting of heritable RNAi (Figure 6B), even when accounting for the exceptionally strong RNAi inheritance in met-2 mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: met-2 mutants were resistant to small RNAs resetting even when weaker RNAi responses were induced and did not show any alteration of the heritable RNAi responses following stress.
source: met-2 mutants were resistant to small RNAs resetting even when weaker RNAi responses were induced and did not show any alteration of the heritable RNAi responses following stress (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MET-2 seems to be required for the execution of resetting of heritable small RNA responses following stress.
source: Overall, MET-2 seems to be required for the execution of resetting of heritable small RNA responses following stress.
evidence: This is a summary statement inferred from the experimental data with met-2 mutants.

claim: Non-DNA-based inheritance could be involved in multiple human disorders.
source: Non-DNA-based inheritance could be involved in multiple human disorders (Crews et al., 2014; Nilsson et al., 2018; Tucci et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: It is still unclear whether the same mechanisms that allow transgenerational inheritance in worms exist in mammals.
source: It is still unclear whether the same mechanisms that allow transgenerational inheritance in worms exist in mammals (Horsthemke, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: If analogous mechanisms to those in worms are conserved in mammals, understanding the pathways that counteract transmission or maintenance of heritable small RNAs could aid in prevention or treatment of various diseases.
source: If analogous mechanisms are indeed conserved, understanding the pathways that counteract transmission or maintenance of heritable small RNAs could aid in prevention or treatment of various diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential translational implications of the findings.
